```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# ---- URPS workforce cross-reference (live from the mufflyaccess SSOT) -------
# The FPMRS/urogynecology footnote cites the 2023 board-certified-active URPS
# workforce from the canonical package (artifact contract 3.0.0) via urps_count(),
# never hardcoded. Fails loud if mufflyaccess is unavailable so the figure can
# never silently drift. NOTE: this makes mufflyaccess a render-time dependency.
if (!requireNamespace("mufflyaccess", quietly = TRUE))
  stop("mufflyaccess (>= 0.10.0) is required to render the URPS workforce cross-reference footnote.")
urps_ct <- function(include_urology, geography = "national")
  as.integer(mufflyaccess::urps_count(
    year = 2023L, measure = "board_certified_active",
    geography = geography, include_urology = include_urology, incomplete = "error"))

# ---- canonical objects (validated on load) ---------------------------------
# run_dir resolves E2SFCA_FROZEN_RUN_ID and fails loudly if the manifest's
# self-declared run_id disagrees (SSOT: scripts/manuscript_e2sfca_values.R).
run_dir <- e2sfca_run_dir(root = here::here())
national_tbl <- load_e2sfca_national_summary(run_dir)
change_tbl   <- e2sfca_specialty_change(national_tbl)
workforce_tbl <- e2sfca_workforce_counts(
  here::here("manuscript", "data", "workforce_counts_2020.csv"),
  national_tbl = national_tbl)   # SSOT: cross-check the staged CSV against the frozen run
disparity_tbl <- e2sfca_disparity_2020(
  here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "figures",
             "allsubspec_2020_inferential_TABLE.csv"))
go_ci_tbl <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "figures",
             "GO_2020_inferential_MC_CI.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
manifest_json <- jsonlite::read_json(
  file.path(run_dir, "e2sfca_run_manifest.json"))
trend_hac <- readRDS(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "figures", "trend_hac.rds"))
trend_hac_tbl <- trend_hac$trend_tbl
go_ratio_trend <- trend_hac$go_ratio
gtr <- function(spec, grp) dplyr::filter(trend_hac_tbl,
  subspecialty == spec, group == grp)
fmt_p_txt <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "NA" else if (p < 0.001) "P<.001" else
  sub("=0\\.", "=.", sprintf(if (p < 0.01) "P=%.3f" else "P=%.2f", p))

# ---- formatters ------------------------------------------------------------
acc3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
acc2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pp1  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
en_dash <- function(x) gsub("(?<=[0-9])-(?=[0-9])", "-", x, perl = TRUE)
intc <- function(x) formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
# Strip the ACS interval from "X (lo-hi)", leaving the point estimate "X" (#7:
# independence makes pooled aggregate ratios' ACS intervals narrower than the
# reported precision, so they are presented as point estimates; see Methods).
point_only <- function(x) sub(" \\(.*\\)$", "", x)
gci  <- function(metric_name) {
  row <- dplyr::filter(go_ci_tbl, metric == metric_name)
  c(point = row$point, lo = row$lo, hi = row$hi)
}
gci_acc <- function(metric_name) {
  v <- gci(metric_name)
  sprintf("%s (95%% CI %s-%s)", acc3(v["point"]), acc3(v["lo"]),
          acc3(v["hi"]))
}
gci_pct <- function(metric_name) {
  v <- gci(metric_name)
  sprintf("%s%% (95%% CI %s-%s)", pp1(v["point"]), pp1(v["lo"]),
          pp1(v["hi"]))
}
spec_chg <- function(spec) dplyr::filter(change_tbl, subspecialty == spec)
spec_wk  <- function(spec) workforce_tbl$n_providers[
  workforce_tbl$subspecialty == spec]

# ---- cross-subspecialty equity summary (2020; drives the equity heatmap) ----
# Group-vs-reference percent difference in 2020 population-weighted access,
# WITHIN each subspecialty, from the canonical stratified series (same source
# behind Figures 3-6). Reference: rurality -> metropolitan; race -> White.
strat_long <- readr::read_csv(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "figures",
  "allsubspec_allyears_stratified_LONG.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
eq20 <- dplyr::filter(strat_long, year == 2020L)
.eq_pct <- function(subs, grp, refstrat) {
  g <- eq20$mean_access[eq20$subspec == subs & eq20$stratum == grp]
  r <- eq20$mean_access[eq20$subspec == subs & eq20$stratum == refstrat]
  100 * (g / r - 1)
}
subs7 <- E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES   # SSOT: scripts/manuscript_e2sfca_values.R
rural_pct <- vapply(subs7, function(s) .eq_pct(s, "Rural", "Metropolitan"), 0)
aian_pct  <- vapply(subs7, function(s)
  .eq_pct(s, "Am. Indian/Alaska Native", "White, non-Hispanic"), 0)
n_rural_lower  <- sum(rural_pct < 0)          # lower access than metro
n_aian_worse   <- sum(aian_pct  < -10)        # materially (>=10%) lower than White
rural_worst    <- names(which.min(rural_pct)) # deepest rural penalty
rural_worst_pct <- min(rural_pct)
rural_min_pen  <- max(rural_pct)              # smallest rural penalty (closest to 0)

# ---- sensitivity analysis (2020 recompute under alternative assumptions) -----
# Canonical: scripts/sensitivity_e2sfca_2020.R re-ran every 2020 surface under
# alternative decay weights, catchment bands, and grid resolution.
sens_tbl  <- readr::read_csv(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "sensitivity",
  "sensitivity_2020.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
sens_base <- dplyr::filter(sens_tbl, variant == "base")
sens_lab  <- c(base = "Sensitivity reference (1,000-m grid)",
  sharper = "Sharper distance decay", slower = "Slower distance decay",
  drop180 = "Drop 180-min band (30/60/120)",
  res500 = "Production resolution (500-m grid)")
sens_summary <- purrr::map_dfr(setdiff(unique(sens_tbl$variant), "base"), function(vn) {
  vv <- dplyr::filter(sens_tbl, variant == vn)
  j  <- dplyr::inner_join(sens_base, vv, by = "subspec", suffix = c("_b", "_v"))
  tibble::tibble(variant = vn,
    rho = suppressWarnings(cor(j$national_b, j$national_v, method = "spearman")),
    rm_med = stats::median(vv$rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),   # magnitude, not just direction
    aw_med = stats::median(vv$aian_white_ratio,  na.rm = TRUE),
    n_rural = sum(vv$rural_metro_ratio < 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_aian  = sum(vv$aian_white_ratio  < 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = nrow(vv))
})
base_rm_med <- stats::median(sens_base$rural_metro_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)  # base rural:metro
base_aw_med <- stats::median(sens_base$aian_white_ratio,  na.rm = TRUE)  # base AIAN:White
sens_rho_identical <- all(abs(sens_summary$rho - 1) < 1e-9)             # ranks identical?

# ---- Figure 7 winsorization (numeric threshold + % of cells clipped) --------
.chg_df <- readRDS(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca_seam", "change_faceted_df.rds"))
chg_dcap <- as.numeric(stats::quantile(abs(.chg_df$diff)[.chg_df$diff != 0],
                                       0.98, na.rm = TRUE))
chg_pct_clipped <- 100 * mean(abs(.chg_df$diff) > chg_dcap, na.rm = TRUE)
rm(.chg_df)  # ~9 MB; drop after computing the two scalars

# ---- cell-level zero-access validation (#6) ---------------------------------
# scripts/cell_level_zero_access_2020.R: direct grid-cell zero-access share vs
# the tract-mean metric. Resolution-stable (500-m and 1,000-m agree to <=0.1 pp

cell_zero_tbl <- readr::read_csv(here::here("artifacts", "2sfca", "cell_zero",
  "cell_zero_2020.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
.cz <- dplyr::filter(cell_zero_tbl, !is.na(diff_pp))
cz_med      <- stats::median(.cz$diff_pp)
cz_max      <- max(.cz$diff_pp)
cz_aian_max <- max(.cz$diff_pp[.cz$group == "Am. Indian/Alaska Native"])
cz_rural_max<- max(.cz$diff_pp[.cz$group == "Rural"])
czval <- function(sub, grp, col)
  cell_zero_tbl[[col]][cell_zero_tbl$subspec == sub & cell_zero_tbl$group == grp][1]

.rz_pt <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(point_only(disparity_tbl$rural_pct_zero)))

cons_loss_area <- 0.00      # % of at-risk population lost under area-weighted allocation

# ---- self-referential word counts: computed LIVE at render, never hardcoded ----
# The precis is fully static, so its count is exact and single-sourced here:
precis_text <- paste(
  "Potential travel-time accessibility to board-certified obstetrics-gynecology",
  "subspecialists shows large, persistent rural and racial disparities, worst for",
  "American Indian or Alaska Native and rural women.")
precis_word_count <- length(strsplit(trimws(precis_text), "\\s+")[[1]])

# Abstract, main-text, and supplement counts are measured from the FINAL knitted
# markdown by a `document` hook (after inline code is evaluated) and substituted in
# for @@...@@ tokens, so a stale literal can never silently ship (cf. the 5,200-word
# drift). Exclusions mirror the audit counter: code, rendered tables, captions,
# citation keys, and subsection headings.
.wc_clean <- function(md) {
  md <- gsub("(?s)```.*?```", " ", md, perl = TRUE)         # fenced code
  md <- gsub("(?s)<table.*?</table>", " ", md, perl = TRUE) # rendered tables
  md <- gsub("(?s)<caption.*?</caption>", " ", md, perl = TRUE)
  md <- gsub("(?s)<!--.*?-->", " ", md, perl = TRUE)        # html comments
  md <- gsub("<[^>]+>", " ", md)                             # remaining html tags
  md <- gsub("\\[[-@;A-Za-z0-9 ]+\\]", " ", md)             # [@cite] keys
  md <- gsub("[#*_>`|]", " ", md)                            # markdown syntax
  md <- gsub("[[:space:]]+", " ", md)
  w <- strsplit(trimws(md), " ")[[1]]; length(w[nzchar(w)])
}
.wc_section <- function(lines, start_re, stop_re) {
  h <- grep("^#{1,3} ", lines)
  st <- h[grepl(start_re, lines[h])]; if (!length(st)) return(NA_integer_)
  s <- st[1]; after <- h[h > s]
  sp <- after[grepl(stop_re, lines[after])]
  e <- if (length(sp)) sp[1] - 1L else length(lines)
  blk <- lines[(s + 1L):e]; blk <- blk[!grepl("^#{1,6} ", blk)]  # drop subsection headings
  .wc_clean(paste(blk, collapse = "\n"))
}
knitr::knit_hooks$set(document = function(x) {
  md <- paste(x, collapse = "\n"); L <- strsplit(md, "\n")[[1]]
  reps <- list(
    "@@ABSTRACT_WC@@" = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Abstract", "^#+ +Introduction"),
    "@@MAIN_WC@@"     = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Introduction",
                          "^#+ +(Supplemental Digital Content|Reproducibility|References)"),
    "@@SUPP_WC@@"     = .wc_section(L, "^#+ +Supplemental Digital Content",
                          "^#+ +(Reproducibility|References)"))
  for (tok in names(reps)) md <- gsub(tok, format(reps[[tok]], big.mark = ","), md, fixed = TRUE)
  md
})
```

```{r diff-distance, include=FALSE}
# Complementary provider-referenced access metric (differential distance, Herb 2021):
# additional straight-line travel to the nearest urogynecologist (FPMRS) beyond the
# nearest general OB/GYN, women 65+. Source: scripts/urps_module_d_differential_distance.R.
.dd_f <- here::here("manuscript", "data", "differential_distance_fpmrs_2026-07-23.csv")
if (file.exists(.dd_f)) {
  .dd <- readr::read_csv(.dd_f, show_col_types = FALSE)
  diff_median_mi <- round(stats::median(.dd$differential_miles, na.rm = TRUE))
  diff_pct_gt30  <- round(100 * sum(.dd$women_65plus[.dd$differential_miles > 30], na.rm = TRUE) /
                          sum(.dd$women_65plus, na.rm = TRUE))
} else { diff_median_mi <- NA_integer_; diff_pct_gt30 <- NA_integer_ }
```

## Abstract {-}

*Précis.* `r precis_text`

**Objective.** To measure geographic access to the seven obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialties across the contiguous United States, `r first_year` to `r last_year`,
and its disparities by rurality and by race and ethnicity.

**Methods.** We located every board-certified subspecialist active in each year and
used modeled road-network travel times (30 to 180 minutes) to measure how reachable
each specialty group was for the 2020 female population (`r intc(pop_2020)` women;
American Community Survey). Potential geographic accessibility was estimated with an
enhanced two-step floating catchment area model, which rewards shorter drives and
accounts for competing demand for the same specialists. We compared access by urban versus rural location and by race
and ethnicity, and described change from `r first_year` to `r primary_last`
(`r last_year` provisional).

**Results.** In 2020, geographic access was highly uneven. About one in five women lived more than a 60-minute drive from the nearest gynecologic oncology
(`r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_60"))`%) or maternal-fetal medicine
(`r pp1(sp("MFM","pct_outside_60"))`%) subspecialist, rising to
`r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_60"))`% for complex family planning; even within a
three-hour drive, `r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_180"))`% remained outside any
complex-family-planning catchment.
Metropolitan women had more than twice the access of rural women (gynecologic
oncology, `r acc2(gci("metro_rural_ratio")["point"])` times as much), and rural women
were about six times as likely to live where no subspecialist was located within the modeled catchment
(`r pp1(gci("rural_zero")["point"])`% vs `r pp1(gci("metro_zero")["point"])`%).
American Indian or Alaska Native women had the highest zero-access share
(`r pp1(gci("zero_aian")["point"])`%), `r pp1(gci("aianzero_minus_whitezero")["point"])`
points higher than non-Hispanic White women. From `r first_year` to
`r primary_last`, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery increased most
(`r pp1(migs_c22$rel_change_pct)`%) and maternal-fetal medicine alone declined
(`r pp1(mfm_c22$rel_change_pct)`%). Disparities held across sensitivity analyses varying decay, catchment, and
resolution.

**Conclusion.** Access to obstetrics-gynecology subspecialists shows large,
persistent rural and racial disparities, greatest for the rarest subspecialties
and for American Indian or Alaska Native and rural women, that narrowed little
over the decade.

## Introduction

Access to advanced obstetric and gynecologic care depends not only on the size of
the workforce but also on where clinicians practice relative to the populations they
serve. The present study evaluates five subspecialties for which the American Board
of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) administers subspecialty certification, complex
family planning, gynecologic oncology, maternal-fetal medicine, reproductive
endocrinology and infertility, and urogynecology and reconstructive pelvic surgery,
and two areas with focused-practice designations, minimally invasive gynecologic
surgery and pediatric and adolescent gynecology. Prior studies suggest substantial
geographic concentration within individual fields: in 2020, 98.3% of gynecologic
oncologists practiced in urban areas [@Desjardins2023]; nearly 40% of
reproductive-aged women lived in areas with limited or no nearby access to assisted
reproductive technology services [@Harris2017]; and a national study of Indian Health
Service locations found a median drive time of 214 minutes to the nearest
obstetric-gynecologic subspecialist [@Akapo2023]. No previous study, however, has
compared potential travel-time accessibility across all seven fields using a common
national framework.

Although geographic proximity is only one of the five dimensions of health care
access [@Penchansky1981; @McLaughlin2002], travel burden can influence whether and
when patients obtain care. Across reproductive health services, longer travel has
been associated with a lower likelihood of timely prenatal-care initiation and fewer
prenatal visits [@Deng2024], with delays or inability to obtain desired abortion care
[@Pleasants2022], and with limited access to fertility treatment [@Harris2017]. In
oncology, greater distance has also been associated with delayed diagnosis, reduced
receipt of appropriate treatment, and worse outcomes [@Ambroggi2015]. Together these
findings establish travel time as a relevant barrier across both oncologic and
nononcologic obstetric and gynecologic care [@Syed2013], while affordability, referral
pathways, insurance coverage, appointment availability, and patient preferences also
shape realized access.

Prior geographic-access research in this area has focused largely on single
subspecialties and on straight-line or county-level distance. Desjardins and
colleagues described county-level, distance-based disparities in potential access
to gynecologic oncologists over 2001-2020 and reported that access did not
improve for rural or American Indian or Alaska Native populations despite a
doubling of the workforce and of fellowship programs [@Desjardins2023]; Ackroyd
and colleagues, using National Provider Identifier records, found that
approximately 91% of U.S. counties had no practicing gynecologic oncologist
[@Ackroyd2021]. More broadly, nearly half of U.S. counties, home to roughly
20 million people, lack any obstetrician-gynecologist [@Chen2026], and travel-time
analyses of individual OB/GYN subspecialty services have found substantial travel
burdens: several million reproductive-aged women live beyond a two-hour drive of an
oncofertility center [@Peipert2023], and a nearest-provider drive-time analysis of
urogynecology access found that barely 1% of U.S. ZIP codes contain a
urogynecologist, with American Indian or Alaska Native women bearing the greatest
travel burden [@Schmidt2024]. These studies, however, characterize access as
county-level presence, a single travel-time threshold, or nearest-provider distance
for one service at a time, none of which accounts for the population competing for a
given subspecialist's time; the authors of the county-level work note that they
cannot distinguish true care deserts from access in an adjacent county [@Chen2026]. Less is known about how
potential accessibility compares across
the full set of OB/GYN subspecialties, how it has changed as the workforce has
entered, retired, and relocated, and how it is distributed by rurality and by
race and ethnicity at a fine geographic scale. The present study advances this
literature in four ways: it spans all seven specialty groups (five ABOG subspecialties
and two focused-practice designations) on one framework;
it measures accessibility as travel time along the actual road network rather than
straight-line or county-centroid distance; it allocates tract-level population to a
500-m computational grid while preserving tract totals, rather than using the county;
and it identifies subspecialists from ABOG certification records, the certification
standard used to define subspecialty, rather than society rosters or provider
registries, computed annually across more than a decade.

We therefore estimated potential spatial accessibility to each of the seven specialty
groups across the contiguous United States from `r first_year` to
`r last_year`, using an enhanced two-step floating catchment area model on
road-network travel-time isochrones with a mass-conserving demand allocation.
Our objectives were to characterize national accessibility levels and their
temporal trends by subspecialty and to quantify disparities by rurality and by
race and ethnicity. Gynecologic oncology was designated a priori as the detailed
exemplar for the stratified disparity analyses, both because it is an oncologic
subspecialty for which timely access is prognostically important and to permit
direct comparison with existing distance-based estimates [@Desjardins2023].

---

## Materials and Methods

### Study design and data sources

This was a retrospective, population-based geospatial analysis of potential
spatial accessibility to the seven American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology
(ABOG)-certified subspecialties across the 48 contiguous United States and the
District of Columbia, `r first_year` through `r last_year`. Subspecialist
identity and board certification were ascertained from ABOG certification data.
Population (demand) came from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey
(ACS) 5-year estimates [@Census2021ACS]; census-tract geometry and demographic
tables were retrieved with the tidycensus interface [@Walker2024], and spatial
operations used the sf and terra frameworks [@Pebesma2018]. Only publicly
available, de-identified aggregate data were used; the study did not involve human
participants and was determined to be exempt from institutional review board
review. [Author to confirm the reviewing IRB and determination number.]

### Subspecialist cohort

For each calendar year, the analytic cohort comprised board-certified
subspecialists who were clinically active in that year. Subspecialty was assigned
from American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) board-certification
records, the certification standard used to define each subspecialty, rather than
from self-reported specialty codes, under which all obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialists are classified as generic obstetrics-gynecology.^[Because
subspecialty is ascertained from ABOG certification, the urogynecology and
reconstructive pelvic surgery (FPMRS) cohort counts only physicians certified
through the ABOG pathway; physicians who entered urogynecology through the
American Board of Urology (ABU) pathway are not captured. The 2020 FPMRS supply in
Table 1 is therefore a single-year, ABOG-only count. For 2023, the
board-certified active urogynecology workforce comprises `r intc(urps_ct(FALSE))`
physicians through the ABOG pathway and `r intc(urps_ct(TRUE) - urps_ct(FALSE))`
ABU net-new physicians (`r intc(urps_ct(TRUE))` nationally and
`r intc(urps_ct(TRUE, "conus"))` in the contiguous United States); the difference
from the 2020 figure reflects the later measure year and the added ABU pathway
rather than a difference in ascertainment.] A physician was
counted as clinically active in year *Y* when their estimated retirement year
exceeded *Y* (strict inequality; retirement was estimated from a multi-source
consensus of practice-activity signals, and certification dated the physician's
entry to the subspecialty), so a physician contributed to a subspecialty's
accessibility surface only in the years in which they were active, and relocations
were tracked so that each physician was placed at their practice location for the
year in question. Each physician was placed at a single practice location per year;
quality-control testing identified no physician-years with multiple concurrent
locations, so no supply was double-counted (eMethods). Physicians were included only
if their practice address geocoded successfully to a contiguous-U.S. location;
unmatched, ungeocoded, or non-contiguous records were excluded. Each specialty
group's supply is therefore a geocoded, contiguous-U.S., clinically-active count
for the year, and will be smaller than a board-certification headcount, which
counts all certificants regardless of clinical activity, successful geocoding, or
location. In 2020,
`r intc(sum(workforce_tbl$n_providers))` subspecialists were active across the seven
specialty groups (Table 1), and the panel comprises `r nrow(national_tbl)`
specialty-year cells (`r n_subspec` groups × `r n_years` years).

### Population, denominators, and geographic units

The demand denominator was the total female population by census tract (ACS table
B01001). The same total-female-population denominator was applied to all seven
subspecialties to yield a reproducible, standardized index; because the
subspecialties serve different age ranges (for example, pediatric and adolescent
gynecology serves children and adolescents, whereas female pelvic medicine and
reconstructive surgery serves a predominantly older population), across-subspecialty
rate comparisons reflect workforce size and clinical scope in addition to access,
and are interpreted accordingly (Discussion). For race and ethnicity, non-Hispanic
White (ACS table B01001H) and Hispanic-origin (any race; B01001I) women
were analyzed alongside race-alone groups (Black, Asian, American Indian or Alaska
Native, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander; B01001B-E); these do not
form a single mutually exclusive partition, because race-alone counts can include
persons of Hispanic origin, so comparisons are among separately defined groups
rather than across a complete classification. Rurality was classified with U.S.
Department of Agriculture Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes [@usda_ruca],
grouping primary codes 1-3 as metropolitan and 4-10 as rural. Census tract vintage
changed between 2019 and 2020; `r first_year`-2019 used 2010-vintage tracts and
2020-`r last_year` used 2020-vintage tracts, each with its contemporaneous ACS
estimates, and a prespecified seam analysis showed that this vintage change had
negligible effects on the national population-weighted estimates under the
mass-conserving production allocator. Because the stratified trends span the
boundary, we also ran a subgroup-specific seam test: holding the 2020 cohort fixed,
we recomputed each subgroup's mean access and zero-access share under the
2010-vintage (2019 ACS) and 2020-vintage (2020 ACS) frameworks; the pure
vintage-induced shift was small for every reported group (median
`r sprintf("%.2f", seam_zero_med)` percentage point in the zero-access share, at most
`r pp1(seam_ra_max)` for rural or American Indian or Alaska Native women, and
`r pp1(seam_zero_max)` at most across all groups, in the small
`r seam_max_grp` group; mean-access shift ≤`r acc3(seam_mean_max)` per 100,000),
indicating the subgroup trends are not artifacts of the tract-vintage change
(Discussion). The analysis was restricted to the 48 contiguous
states and the District of Columbia; Alaska was therefore excluded, which is
relevant to interpretation of the American Indian or Alaska Native findings
(Discussion). The 2020 analysis represented `r intc(pop_2020)` women.

### Travel-time isochrones

Drive-time isochrones of 30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes were generated around each
physician practice location with the Valhalla routing engine on OpenStreetMap
road networks [@Valhalla2023]. We deliberately held the routing network constant
across all study years, rather than re-routing on a per-year network, so that
year-to-year change in the accessible footprint reflects only the change in the
active physician cohort and not incidental differences in the road extract; the
OpenStreetMap extract and Valhalla tiles were built from a single snapshot
(*[extract date to be confirmed by the authors]*). Holding the network fixed is a
design choice to isolate the cohort effect, not a claim that road travel conditions
were unchanged over the study period.

### Enhanced two-step floating catchment area accessibility

Potential spatial accessibility was estimated with the enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) method [@luoqi2009; @luowang2003], using road-network travel time and a Gaussian distance-decay across the four bands (weights `r manifest_json$weights[["30"]]`, `r manifest_json$weights[["60"]]`, `r manifest_json$weights[["120"]]`, and `r manifest_json$weights[["180"]]` for 30/60/120/180 minutes). Supply is the count of distinct active subspecialists at each location; accessibility is a relative index (subspecialists per 100,000 women) and, equivalently, a Spatial Access Ratio normalized to the national mean of 1.00 [@Wan2012spar], the absolute per-100,000 value retained alongside it. Because the same weights enter both steps, the national population-weighted mean reduces algebraically to supply per population (a conservation property) and is reported only as a standardized workforce index; spatial variation resides in the *distribution* of the surface (rurality and race/ethnicity contrasts, the share outside the catchment, and geographic inequality), which we treat as the primary spatial outcomes. The full algorithm, the incremental-band derivation and provider-to-population and accessibility equations, the weight rationale, and the alternative-specification sensitivity framework (Gaussian-derived zonal reparameterization, variable urban/rural catchments, and an M2SFCA maldistribution penalty) are in eMethods S4.

### Mass-conserving demand allocation

Demand was allocated from census tracts to a 500-m equal-area grid (EPSG:5070) by polygon-cell area overlap, conserving every tract's population (`r cons_pct(cons_loss_area)`% loss vs `r cons_pct(cons_loss_centroid)`% under centroid allocation); the 500-m and 1,000-m surfaces gave near-identical results. The method assumes uniform within-tract density, least tenable in large rural and tribal tracts; detail is in eMethods S2.

### Temporal comparison

National accessibility was computed for every subspecialty-year cell; the `r first_year`-`r last_year` comparison surfaces were computed on a single common grid and denominator (2020 vintage; ACS 2020) so the difference reflects only the change in the active cohort (eMethods S3).

### Statistical analysis

National accessibility was summarized as the population-weighted mean at the raster-cell level, with intervals reflecting only ACS sampling error; because the physician catchments are deterministic and tracts were treated as independent, pooled intervals are near-zero-width and are reported as point estimates whose honest uncertainty envelope is the sensitivity range. Temporal change was summarized by ordinary least-squares slopes with Newey-West HAC P values, excluding the most recent (right-censored) year; stratified trend analyses are exploratory. Full detail on the uncertainty model, the zero-access estimators, the trend specification, and the robustness analyses is in eMethods S1. Analyses used R version `r manifest_json$environment$r_version`.

---

## Results

### Subspecialist workforce and study population

We identified board-certified obstetrics-gynecology subspecialists active in each
year from `r first_year` through `r last_year` and modeled potential spatial
accessibility with an enhanced two-step floating catchment area method
[@luoqi2009; @luowang2003] for the `r intc(pop_2020)` women represented by the
2020 American Community Survey [@Census2021ACS] across the 48 contiguous United
States and the District of Columbia. In 2020, the active
workforce comprised `r intc(spec_wk("MFM"))` maternal-fetal medicine (MFM),
`r intc(spec_wk("GO"))` gynecologic oncology (GO), `r intc(spec_wk("REI"))`
reproductive endocrinology and infertility (REI), `r intc(spec_wk("FPMRS"))`
female pelvic medicine and reconstructive surgery (FPMRS; urogynecology),
`r intc(spec_wk("MIGS"))` minimally invasive gynecologic surgery (MIGS),
`r intc(spec_wk("PAG"))` pediatric and adolescent gynecology (PAG), and
`r intc(spec_wk("CFP"))` complex family planning (CFP) physicians. Because the
area-weighted demand allocation preserved the full modeled population total (`r cons_pct(cons_loss_area)`%
loss, vs `r cons_pct(cons_loss_centroid)`% under conventional centroid allocation), each tract's
modeled female population total was retained in the accessibility estimates (Table 1).

```{r table1}
abbr_note <- paste0("AIAN, American Indian or Alaska Native; CFP, complex family ",
  "planning; FPMRS, female pelvic medicine and reconstructive surgery; GO, ",
  "gynecologic oncology; MFM, maternal-fetal medicine; MIGS, minimally invasive ",
  "gynecologic surgery; PAG, pediatric and adolescent gynecology; REI, ",
  "reproductive endocrinology and infertility.")
tbl1 <- workforce_tbl |>
  dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, physicians = n_providers) |>
  dplyr::left_join(national_tbl |> dplyr::filter(year == 2020L) |>
    dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, access = mean_pop_weighted_per100k),
    by = "subspecialty") |>
  dplyr::left_join(change_tbl_22 |>
    dplyr::transmute(subspecialty, relc = rel_change_pct), by = "subspecialty") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(access)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = subspecialty,
    `Active physicians, 2020` = formatC(physicians, format = "d", big.mark = ","),
    `Supply per 100,000, 2020` = sprintf("%.3f", access),
    `Change, 2013-2022` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", relc))
knitr::kable(tbl1, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste0("Table 1. Active Workforce and Standardized Supply per ",
    "Population by Obstetrics-Gynecology Subspecialty, 2020")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
                            font_size = 12, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "Active physicians are the 2020 board-certified, contiguous-U.S., geocoded ",
    "provider counts. The supply-per-population column is the national ",
    "population-weighted mean of the enhanced two-step floating catchment area ",
    "surface, which by a conservation property of the method equals subspecialist ",
    "supply per 100,000 women (Methods); it is a standardized ",
    "workforce-distribution index, not a spatial-accessibility measure, and its ",
    "ranking is the workforce-size ranking. Spatial distribution and disparities ",
    "are reported in Tables 2-3 and Figures 3-6. Change is the ",
    "descriptive relative change from ", first_year, " to ",
    primary_last, "; ", last_year, " is right-censored and reported provisionally. ",
    "Trend inference is given in Appendix Table S1. ", abbr_note))
```

### Spatial distribution and inequality of access

Because the national population-weighted mean is algebraically a
supply-per-population index and carries no spatial information (Methods), we report
the *geographic distribution* of access as the primary description. Potential
accessibility in 2020 was strongly concentrated in metropolitan areas of
the eastern and midwestern United States, with large contiguous regions of the
Mountain West and Great Plains lying outside the catchment of any subspecialist;
the scarcest subspecialties, complex family planning and pediatric and adolescent
gynecology, showed geographically extensive areas of zero modeled access, covering
most of the land area outside major metropolitan regions (Figure 1).

```{r figlevel}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig0_level2020.jpg"))
```
**Figure 1.** Potential spatial accessibility to each obstetrics-gynecology
subspecialty, 2020, per 100,000 women, estimated with an enhanced
two-step floating catchment area model on 30-, 60-, 120-, and 180-minute
travel-time isochrones. Brighter shading indicates greater potential accessibility;
black indicates no modeled access (a desert). One panel per subspecialty on a
shared square-root color scale (capped at the 98th percentile); the number in each
label is the national population-weighted mean. Mass-conserving 500-m demand grid
aggregated to a 1,000-m display surface; contiguous United States.

Quantifying that distribution, in 2020 roughly one in five women lived
outside a 60-minute drive of the nearest subspecialist for the more common
fields, `r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_60"))`% for gynecologic oncology,
`r pp1(sp("MFM","pct_outside_60"))`% for maternal-fetal medicine, and
`r pp1(sp("FPMRS","pct_outside_60"))`% for female pelvic medicine, rising to
`r pp1(sp("PAG","pct_outside_60"))`% for pediatric and adolescent gynecology and
`r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_60"))`% for complex family planning (Table 2). Even
within a three-hour drive, `r pp1(sp("CFP","pct_outside_180"))`% of women remained
outside any complex-family-planning catchment and `r pp1(sp("PAG","pct_outside_180"))`%
outside any pediatric and adolescent gynecology catchment, versus
`r pp1(sp("GO","pct_outside_180"))`% for gynecologic oncology. The spatial
concentration of access, summarized by the population-weighted Gini index, was
lowest for `r full_name[sp_gini_min_sub]` (`r acc2(sp_gini_min)`) and highest for
`r full_name[sp_gini_max_sub]` (`r acc2(sp_gini_max)`), indicating that the scarcest
fields are not only smaller but far more unevenly distributed (Table 2).

```{r table2sp}
sp_tab <- spatial_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(subspec = factor(subspec,
    levels = E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES)) |>   # SSOT display order
  dplyr::arrange(subspec) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = subspec,
    `% outside 60 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_60),
    `% outside 120 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_120),
    `% outside 180 min` = sprintf("%.1f", pct_outside_180),
    `Gini` = sprintf("%.2f", gini))
knitr::kable(sp_tab, align = c("l","r","r","r","r"),
  caption = paste0("Table 2. Spatial Distribution and Inequality of Potential ",
    "Accessibility by Subspecialty, 2020")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","condensed"),
                            font_size = 12, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "“% outside t min” is the share of women with no subspecialist ",
    "reachable within a t-minute drive (population-weighted, road-network ",
    "travel time). Gini is the population-weighted Gini index of the accessibility ",
    "surface (0 = perfectly even; higher = more spatially concentrated). These are ",
    "spatial-distribution measures and, unlike the standardized supply index in ",
    "Table 1, depend on provider geography. Computed on a 1-km demand grid. ",
    abbr_note))
```

On the common denominator, the standardized supply index (Table 1) was highest for
maternal-fetal medicine and lowest for complex family planning (Figure 2A); because
this index equals workforce supply per population (Methods), it reflects workforce
size and clinical scope rather than spatial access and is not comparable across
subspecialties.


`r first_year`-`r last_year` (E2SFCA on travel-time isochrones). (A)
Population-weighted accessibility by subspecialty, 2020. (B) By subspecialty,

### Temporal trends

From `r first_year` to `r primary_last` (the primary period; `r last_year` was
right-censored and is reported provisionally), minimally invasive gynecologic
surgery increased from `r acc3(migs_c22[["y2013"]])` to
`r acc3(migs_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])` per 100,000 women (a
`r pp1(migs_c22$rel_change_pct)`% relative change), the largest relative increase
among the subspecialties, and maternal-fetal medicine was the only subspecialty to
decline (`r acc3(mfm_c22[["y2013"]])` to
`r acc3(mfm_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])`; `r pp1(mfm_c22$rel_change_pct)`%),
reaching a mid-series low of `r acc3(mfm_c22$series_min)` in
`r mfm_c22$series_min_year`. Gynecologic oncology increased from
`r acc3(go_c22[["y2013"]])` to `r acc3(go_c22[[paste0("y", primary_last)]])`
(`r pp1(go_c22$rel_change_pct)`%). Each annual estimate used only physicians active
in that year, reflecting retirement, new board certification, and relocation
(Figure 2B). On a provisional basis, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery reached
`r acc3(migs_c[["y2023"]])` and maternal-fetal medicine `r acc3(mfm_c[["y2023"]])`
per 100,000 women in `r last_year`.

### Disparities by rurality

For gynecologic oncology in 2020, population-weighted accessibility was
`r acc2(gci("metro_mean")["point"])` per 100,000 women in metropolitan
areas versus `r acc2(gci("rural_mean")["point"])` in rural areas, a
metropolitan-to-rural ratio of `r acc2(gci("metro_rural_ratio")["point"])`
(Figure 3A; ACS uncertainty intervals for all estimates appear in Table 3). At the
extreme of no access, `r pp1(gci("rural_zero")["point"])`% of rural women lived in a census tract whose mean modeled access to a gynecologic
oncologist was zero, versus `r pp1(gci("metro_zero")["point"])`% of metropolitan
women, an approximately sixfold higher rate.

### Disparities by race and ethnicity

American Indian or Alaska Native women had the lowest gynecologic
oncology accessibility (`r acc3(gci("mean_aian")["point"])` per 100,000) and the
highest share living in census tracts with zero mean modeled access
(`r pp1(gci("zero_aian")["point"])`%); the zero-access share was
`r pp1(gci("aianzero_minus_whitezero")["point"])` percentage points higher than for
non-Hispanic White women (ACS uncertainty interval excluding zero).
Asian women had the highest modeled accessibility (Figure 3B). Because
race-alone and Hispanic-origin groups do not form a mutually exclusive
classification (Methods), these are comparisons among separately defined groups.

```{r fig3}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig3_go2020.jpg"))
```
**Figure 3.** Gynecologic oncology accessibility in 2020 by (A) rurality and (B)
race and ethnicity, population-weighted per 100,000 women. "% zero" = share of the
group's population living in census tracts whose mean modeled access to a
gynecologic oncologist is zero (a tract-level, not individual-level, measure).

### Disparities across all subspecialties

The rurality and race/ethnicity disparities were directionally consistent across all seven specialty groups; per-subspecialty estimates are reported in eResults S5.

### Persistence of disparities over time

The rural and racial disparities persisted with little narrowing across `r first_year`-`r last_year`; the year-by-year detail is in eResults S6.

### Access deserts across subspecialties

The share of women outside any modeled catchment ("access deserts") varied widely by subspecialty; per-subspecialty values are in eResults S7.

---

### Change in accessibility by subspecialty

Decade-scale change differed by subspecialty, minimally invasive gynecologic surgery increased most and maternal-fetal medicine alone declined; the per-subspecialty change is in eResults S8.

## Discussion

In this national analysis of potential spatial accessibility to the seven
ABOG-certified obstetric and gynecologic subspecialties, accessibility was
consistently concentrated in metropolitan areas and lowest for rural women and
for American Indian or Alaska Native women, and these disparities changed
little across the study period. The subspecialties differed markedly in absolute accessibility and in their
temporal trajectories.

These findings extend prior geographic-access research, which has largely examined
single subspecialties or straight-line, county-level distance. For gynecologic
oncology, our results reproduce and refine the county-level, straight-line two-step
floating catchment model of Desjardins and colleagues, who found most gynecologic
oncologists in urban counties, 95.2% of counties (roughly 54.7 million at-risk
women) with none, and, critically, no improvement over two decades in the share of
American Indian or Alaska Native women beyond 100 miles (25.6% to 23.7%; P=.866)
[@Desjardins2023]. Our year-specific, board-certified cohort is smaller by design,
so the counts are not directly comparable, but our travel-time, tract-level surface
independently corroborates the same inequities at finer resolution and across all
seven specialty groups. A state-level E2SFCA analysis similarly found 18.4% of Georgia
tracts with zero access and, by combining spatial access with social vulnerability,
doubly disadvantaged communities invisible to either measure alone [@Graham2019],
the logic behind our stratified, group-versus-reference synthesis (Figure 4).

A complementary, provider-referenced metric reinforces this for female pelvic
medicine and reconstructive surgery. Using differential distance, the extra travel
to the nearest urogynecologist beyond the nearest general obstetrician-gynecologist,
against more than 40,000 geocoded general obstetrician-gynecologists [@Herb2021],
women 65 or older in the median county faced roughly `r diff_median_mi` additional
miles, and `r diff_pct_gt30`% lived where this marginal burden exceeded 30 miles,
concentrated in the rural Plains and Mountain West. By isolating the incremental
cost of *needing* a subspecialist, it shows that subspecialty maldistribution,
rather than an absence of gynecologic care, drives the rural access gap.

Our other-subspecialty findings are likewise consistent with the literature. The
extensive reproductive endocrinology and infertility zero-access areas echo estimates
that roughly 29% of reproductive-aged U.S. women live without an assisted reproductive
technology clinic, with well-documented racial and ethnic disparities [@Beroukhim2023],
and an oncofertility travel-time analysis found the share beyond a two-hour drive
nearly doubled from general to subspecialized fertility care (3.4% to 5.7%),
paralleling our deeper deserts in narrower subspecialties [@Peipert2023]. These
literatures emphasize that such disparities are multifactorial, the Disparities in
Assisted Reproductive Technology framework attributes them to delayed presentation,
discontinuation, provider, and patient-level factors beyond structural access
[@Seifer2022], framing how our geographic measure should be read.

The persistence of these disparities is consistent with access gradients documented
across many specialized services, including cardiac rehabilitation, transplantation,
pediatric and specialized cancer care, lung-cancer screening, mental health, and
rehabilitation therapy, where rural and American Indian or Alaska Native populations
are consistently farther from care [@Ebinger2022; @Yilma2023; @Liu2023; @Towne2014;
@ElKhoury2024; @Hecox2026; @Welch2024; @Campbell2025; @Charlesworth2024]. The most
comparable prior work, a national E2SFCA analysis of six dental specialties,
reproduced our central patterns: more than 98% of specialists urban and rural
people in rural areas driving roughly three times as far [@Rahman2026]. Subspecialists cluster
in metropolitan academic and referral centers, and many rural regions, and areas
with large American Indian or Alaska Native populations, lie beyond even a 180-minute
drive of any, so incremental workforce growth need not reach them; indeed the
workforce grew over the study period even as rural and American Indian or Alaska
Native access held nearly constant. The findings thus indicate a persistent geographic
mismatch between specialist locations and the populations potentially seeking care, and
because the denominator is total population rather than
disease or procedure demand, these estimates locate where the geographic component
of access is most deficient, not where clinical need is greatest. Narrowing the gaps
therefore likely requires strategies that decouple access from physician relocation,
such as hub-and-spoke models, telehealth, provider knowledge-sharing networks like
Project ECHO [@Arora2023], placement incentives such as the National Health Service
Corps, and visiting-specialist clinics, each warranting formal evaluation rather
than presumed benefit. Because our measure captures potential rather than realized
access, its value is in identifying where such strategies are most needed.

Potential accessibility is not a surrogate for realized use or outcomes: of the five
dimensions of access, the model captures only availability and geographic
accessibility [@Penchansky1981; @McLaughlin2002], not affordability, accommodation,
or acceptability. Populations with high modeled proximity can still fare poorly, as
groups near referral centers may register favorable access yet face systemic racism,
insurance and scheduling barriers, and higher disease burden [@Bassett2020]. This
metropolitan concentration, and its reversal outside metros where minority
populations fare worse, mirrors the race-by-rurality intersection reported for
emergency surgical services [@McCrum2022] and mammography access [@Campbell2026];
and because racial outcome disparities attenuate after adjustment for structural
factors such as insurance, income, and education [@Greenberg2023], a geographic
access difference becomes an inequity when patterned by unequally distributed social
factors, most pronounced where low socioeconomic status and isolation coincide
[@Hod2014]. Modeled proximity should therefore be read as one necessary but
insufficient condition for equitable care, its use being to localize where the
geographic gap is deepest rather than to certify adequacy where proximity is high.

The study has several strengths: a near-census of board-certified subspecialists
rather than a sample; road-network travel times rather than straight-line distance;
a mass-conserving demand allocation that represented the full female population
rather than discarding population near tract centroids, mitigating the distance-type
and population-aggregation errors documented for potential-access measures
[@Apparicio2017]; year-specific active
cohorts that reflect real workforce entry, exit, and relocation; and fully
reproducible, canonical-source computation of every reported value. Unlike
nearest-provider travel time or administrative-area provider ratios, the
floating-catchment design jointly incorporates provider availability, competing
population demand, and travel impedance, and flags low-access areas that those
simpler measures do not [@Drake2021].

Several limitations temper interpretation. The same total-female-population denominator was applied to all seven specialty groups, so across-subspecialty comparisons reflect workforce size and clinical scope as well as access; the index measures potential rather than realized access and omits practice capacity, appointment availability, insurance, and patient travel behavior; the reported intervals capture only ACS sampling error and are therefore not comprehensive confidence intervals; the zero-access metric is defined at the tract level; race-alone and Hispanic-origin groups do not form a mutually exclusive partition; and Alaska's exclusion limits generalizability to the full U.S. American Indian or Alaska Native population and omits Alaska Native communities with distinct transportation barriers. These points, together with international-border edge effects, the uniform-within-tract density assumption of the area-weighted allocation, and directions for empirical patient-flow calibration, are detailed in eDiscussion S9.

## Conclusion

Across the contiguous United States, potential accessibility to board-certified
obstetric and
gynecologic subspecialists was persistently lower for rural women and for
American Indian or Alaska Native women, and these disparities narrowed little
over more than a decade. Interpreted as a measure of where specialized care is
potentially reachable, rather than of realized or clinically sufficient access, these
findings identify the populations and regions that may benefit most from
regionalized care, outreach, telehealth, and targeted workforce strategies.

## Supplemental Digital Content {-}


## eMethods S1: Statistical analysis {-}

National accessibility was summarized as the population-weighted mean at the
raster-cell level. Uncertainty intervals reflect only sampling error in the ACS
population weights: because the physician catchments and cell-level accessibility
values are deterministic (a near-census of active physicians on fixed isochrones),
we propagated the ACS margins of error by Monte-Carlo simulation (2,000 draws;
each tract's female population drawn from a Normal distribution with SD = margin of
error ÷ 1.645) and summarized each estimate by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
Draws were not truncated at zero: because they enter only aggregate weighted sums
(where the expectation equals the sum of the tract estimates), clamping would inject
spurious positive weight into the many zero-population tracts and bias sparse groups
(for example, American Indian or Alaska Native) upward. Tracts were treated as
independent, so the variance of an aggregate is the sum of tract variances; this
does not use the ACS covariance structure or replicate weights, and because errors
average out across the tens of thousands of tracts, the intervals for pooled
quantities, especially aggregate ratios such as the metropolitan-to-rural
ratio, collapse to implausibly narrow ranges. Such intervals should be read as point
estimates whose honest uncertainty envelope is the sensitivity range (Appendix
Table S2) rather than as informative confidence intervals; we accordingly report a
point estimate alone where the interval is narrower than the reported precision. We
refer to these
as ACS uncertainty intervals; they do not incorporate uncertainty from physician
ascertainment, clinical-activity classification, geocoding, multiple practice
locations, practice capacity, travel-time modeling, catchment thresholds, or
distance-decay weights, and are therefore narrower than a comprehensive confidence
interval would be. Rurality- and race/ethnicity-stratified estimates were computed
at the tract level (required to attach RUCA rurality and race-specific
denominators) and reconcile with the cell-level national summary to within 0.001
per 100,000 women. The zero-access metric (“% zero”) is the share of a
group’s population living in census tracts whose mean modeled access is zero. As a
sensitivity comparison, we also computed a cell-level estimator for 2020, the
area-weighted share of each tract lying in grid cells with zero access, weighted by
the tract's group population, which was stable between the 500-m and 1,000-m grids
(agreement within 0.1 percentage point for the subspecialties checked) and gave
higher zero-access shares than the tract-mean definition (Appendix Table S3).
Because both estimators rest on the same area-weighted (uniform within-tract
density) allocation, this difference reflects the choice of definition, not
independent evidence that either value is more accurate; a dasymetric or block-level
allocation would be required to establish that (Discussion). A subspecialist was considered reachable if the practice location
fell within the 180-minute maximum travel-time catchment. Temporal change was
summarized by ordinary least-squares slopes of the annual estimate on calendar year
over `r first_year`-`r primary_last`. Because successive ACS 5-year estimates
overlap and provider cohorts are serially correlated, we also computed Newey-West
heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) P values, with the lag
prespecified at `r trend_hac$hac_lag` to reflect the overlap of the 5-year ACS
window (Appendix Table S1); because only 10 annual estimates were available, these
trend tests are imprecise and are interpreted descriptively. The stratified trend
analyses across the seven specialty groups and multiple groups are exploratory: we
prespecified no primary comparison and applied no multiple-comparisons correction,
and we therefore emphasize the direction and magnitude of change over statistical
significance. The most recent year (`r last_year`) was excluded from trend
estimation and is reported as a provisional observation because its workforce panel
is subject to right-censoring. To assess robustness to modeling choices, we
recomputed the 2020 accessibility surface for every subspecialty under alternative
distance-decay weights (sharper and slower falloff), a reduced catchment (dropping
the 180-minute band), and a finer 500-m grid, and compared the national ranking and
the rurality and race contrasts with the base specification (Appendix Table S2).
Analyses used R version `r manifest_json$environment$r_version`.

## eMethods S2: Mass-conserving demand allocation {-}

Demand was allocated from census tracts to a 500-m equal-area analysis grid
(EPSG:5070) by polygon-cell area overlap, conserving every tract's population
(mass-conserving area-weighted allocation). This preserved each tract's modeled
population total (`r cons_pct(cons_loss_area)`% loss) versus a `r cons_pct(cons_loss_centroid)`% loss under conventional centroid-based
allocation; per-year national totals were conserved to within 10⁻⁶. Conserving
population prevents the loss that centroid allocation incurs and reduces the
display-scale aggregation that coarser zone centroids impose [@BryantDelamater2019];
it does not, however, improve the underlying spatial precision, because population
is distributed by land-area overlap and the method therefore assumes uniform
population density within each tract. This assumption is least tenable in large
rural and tribal tracts, where women occupy a small fraction of the land area,
so the 500-m surface can appear more spatially precise than the tract-level input
justifies (see Limitations). The 500-m and 1,000-m surfaces nonetheless gave
near-identical results (Appendix Table S2).

## eMethods S3: Temporal comparison, 2013-2023 {-}

National accessibility was computed for every subspecialty-year cell. To visualize
decade-scale change while isolating the cohort effect, the `r first_year` and
`r last_year` accessibility surfaces for each subspecialty were computed on a
single common grid and demand denominator (2020 tract vintage; ACS 2020), so the
difference reflects only the change in the active physician cohort.


*Appendix 1. Accessibility change by subspecialty, `r first_year`-`r last_year`
(to be posted online as Supplemental Digital Content).*

Level maps look similar year-to-year because the workforce is ~85-95% persistent
between consecutive years; the change accumulates. To isolate the cohort signal,
each figure below computes the `r first_year` and `r last_year` surfaces on one
common grid (2020 tract vintage; ACS 2020), so the difference (panel C) reflects
only the change in the active physician cohort. Red = access grew; blue = shrank.
Because both years are placed on the 2020 grid, the national means and percentage
changes annotated on these figures are computed on that common (cohort-isolated)
basis and differ by up to about 5 percentage points from the vintage-matched
canonical national changes reported in the Results, Table 1, and Figure 7; those
canonical values (e.g., minimally invasive gynecologic surgery
`r sprintf("%+.0f%%", migs_c$rel_change_pct)`, maternal-fetal medicine
`r sprintf("%+.0f%%", mfm_c$rel_change_pct)`) are the authoritative national
estimates, and these appendix figures are provided to show the underlying spatial
pattern and the 2013 baseline versus 2023 endpoint.

*Appendix 2. Sensitivity of the 2020 findings to modeling assumptions.*

The 2020 accessibility surface for each subspecialty was recomputed under
alternative distance-decay weights (sharper and slower falloff than the base
Gaussian weights), a reduced catchment that dropped the 180-minute band, and the
production 500-m grid (the sensitivity was computed on a 1,000-m reference grid for
efficiency; the 500-m specification reproduces the resolution that generated the
production national values). The national population-weighted mean and its induced
subspecialty ranking were identical across every specification (Spearman
`r if (sens_rho_identical) "ρ = 1.00" else sprintf("ρ ≥ %.2f", sens_min_rho)`); this
is *not* evidence of spatial robustness but a direct consequence of the conservation
property (Methods), the national mean equals supply divided by population and does
not depend on the decay weights, catchment bands, or grid resolution. The meaningful
sensitivity is therefore in the *spatial* quantities. Rural women had lower
accessibility
than metropolitan women for all `r sens_n` subspecialties under every
specification. American Indian or Alaska Native women had lower accessibility
than non-Hispanic White women for all `r sens_n` subspecialties under the
base, sharper-decay, dropped-band, and production-resolution specifications, and for
`r min(sens_summary$n_aian)` of `r sens_n` under the slowest decay (complex family
planning, already near parity, crossed to a slight advantage). Magnitudes did move, and Table S2
reports them: the median rural:metro accessibility ratio was `r acc2(base_rm_med)`
at the reference specification and ranged from `r acc2(min(sens_summary$rm_med))`
(sharper decay; deeper rural gap) to `r acc2(max(sens_summary$rm_med))` (slower
decay; shallower gap), while the median AIAN:White ratio moved only within
`r acc2(min(sens_summary$aw_med))`-`r acc2(max(sens_summary$aw_med))`
(reference `r acc2(base_aw_med)`); direction never reversed, and the
production-resolution (500-m) grid reproduced the reference results almost exactly. This insensitivity
of direction to the distance-decay weights is consistent with prior
enhanced two-step floating catchment area analyses, including studies of mental
health and of maternal-health services, in which access estimates were
likewise robust to varying the decay parameter [@Charlesworth2024; @Vadrevu2016].

```{r tableS2}
tblS2 <- sens_summary |>
  dplyr::transmute(Specification = sens_lab[variant],
    `Rank ρ` = sprintf("%.2f", rho),
    `Rural:metro ratio (median)` = sprintf("%.2f", rm_med),
    `AIAN:White ratio (median)` = sprintf("%.2f", aw_med),
    `Rural < metro` = sprintf("%d/%d", n_rural, n),
    `AIAN < White` = sprintf("%d/%d", n_aian, n))
knitr::kable(tblS2, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
  caption = paste0("Appendix Table S2. Sensitivity of 2020 Findings to Modeling ",
    "Assumptions (Seven Specialty Groups)")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
                            font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "Each 2020 accessibility surface was recomputed under the listed specification ",
    "and compared with the reference specification (Gaussian band weights ",
    manifest_json$weights[["30"]], "/", manifest_json$weights[["60"]], "/",
    manifest_json$weights[["120"]], "/", manifest_json$weights[["180"]],
    " for the 30/60/120/180-minute bands). The sensitivity was computed on a ",
    "1,000-m reference grid for efficiency; the production/authoritative national ",
    "values use a 500-m grid (Methods), reproduced by the 'Production resolution' ",
    "row. Rank ρ is the Spearman correlation of the seven specialty groups' national ",
    "population-weighted mean accessibility with the reference ranking (reference ",
    "median rural:metro ratio ", sprintf("%.2f", base_rm_med), ", AIAN:White ratio ",
    sprintf("%.2f", base_aw_med), "). The ratio columns are the median across the ",
    "seven specialty groups; a ratio below 1 means the disadvantaged group had lower ",
    "accessibility. “Rural < metro” and “AIAN < White” count the subspecialties in ",
    "which that held. ", abbr_note))
```

*Appendix 3. Cell-level versus tract-level zero-access, 2020.*

The zero-access share reported throughout is defined at the census-tract level (the
share of a group's population in tracts whose *mean* modeled access is zero). As a
sensitivity comparison, a cell-level estimator was computed for 2020: for each
tract, the area-weighted fraction lying in 500-m grid cells with zero access,
aggregated by the tract's group population. The cell-level estimate exceeded the
tract-mean estimate for every group and subspecialty (median
+`r pp1(cz_med)` percentage points; maximum +`r pp1(cz_max)`), and the divergence
was largest for the most disadvantaged groups. Because both estimators assume
uniform population density within each tract, this comparison shows only that the
two definitions differ, not that either is the more accurate estimate of the true
burden; a dasymetric or block-level allocation would be needed to adjudicate.
Values agreed between the 500-m and 1,000-m grids to within 0.1 percentage point.

```{r tableS3}
czw <- cell_zero_tbl |>
  dplyr::filter(group %in% c("Metropolitan","Rural","White, non-Hispanic",
                             "Am. Indian/Alaska Native")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(g = dplyr::recode(group, "Metropolitan"="Metro", "Rural"="Rural",
    "White, non-Hispanic"="White", "Am. Indian/Alaska Native"="AIAN"),
    cell = sprintf("%.1f", cell_zero_pct), tract = sprintf("%.1f", tract_zero_pct)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(subspec, g, cell_tract = paste0(cell, " / ", tract)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = g, values_from = cell_tract) |>
  dplyr::mutate(subspec = factor(subspec,
    levels = E2SFCA_SUBSPECIALTIES)) |>   # SSOT display order
  dplyr::arrange(subspec) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Subspecialty = subspec, Metro, Rural, White, AIAN)
knitr::kable(czw, align = c("l","r","r","r","r"),
  caption = paste0("Appendix Table S3. Cell-Level vs Tract-Level Zero-Access ",
    "Share (%), 2020 (cell / tract)")) |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","condensed"),
                            font_size = 11, full_width = TRUE) |>
  kableExtra::footnote(general_title = "", threeparttable = TRUE, general = paste0(
    "Each cell shows the cell-level zero-access share / the tract-level share (%). ",
    "Cell-level is the group-population-weighted mean of each tract's area fraction ",
    "in 500-m grid cells with zero modeled access; tract-level is the share in ",
    "tracts whose mean access is zero. Both estimators assume uniform within-tract ",
    "density, so the higher cell-level values reflect the definition, not evidence ",
    "that either is more accurate. ", abbr_note))
```

## eMethods S4: Enhanced two-step floating catchment area, algorithm, weights, and sensitivity {-}

Potential spatial accessibility was estimated with the enhanced two-step floating
catchment area (E2SFCA) method [@luoqi2009], an extension of the two-step floating
catchment area approach [@luowang2003] that is now widely applied to physician,
screening, surgical, and other health-service access [@Gilliland2019;
@Wurdeman2026; @Welch2024; @Campbell2025; @Charlesworth2024; @Utaka2026;
@Petzold2025; @Arora2025], and a recent systematic review situates them within the broader gravity-model family of potential spatial-access measures [@Stacherl2023]. Floating catchment methods were chosen over
crude provider-to-population ratios, which ignore where supply sits relative to
demand and capture a distinct dimension of access that binary distance or
travel-time thresholds undercount [@Nakamura2017; @SanchezCardenas2024;
@McCrum2022], and travel time along the road network was used
rather than straight-line distance, which overstates reachability where terrain or
road structure lengthens the true trip [@Ebinger2022]. Demand within each catchment
was weighted
by a Gaussian distance-decay across the four travel-time bands (weights
`r manifest_json$weights[["30"]]`, `r manifest_json$weights[["60"]]`,
`r manifest_json$weights[["120"]]`, and `r manifest_json$weights[["180"]]` for the
30-, 60-, 120-, and 180-minute zones); these Gaussian band weights follow the
published E2SFCA formulation and match values in common use (the inner-band weights
are identical to those applied in recent screening-access studies), and a slower
distance decay with a wider catchment is appropriate for specialized care that
patients travel farther to reach than primary care [@luoqi2009; @Campbell2025];
studies contrasting generalist and subspecialty access likewise assign
subspecialists materially wider catchments than primary care providers
[@Liu2026].
No single distance-decay function is empirically established as correct, and the
floating-catchment literature has called for finer spatial demand units and refined
decay functions than the coarse zone centroids and step weights used in most prior
work [@Hong2023; @Weng2025]; we therefore resolved demand on a fine grid, adopted
the conventional Gaussian weights, and confirmed that the findings were insensitive
to this choice, to the catchment bands, and to the grid resolution in a sensitivity
analysis (Appendix Table S2). That sensitivity framework additionally supports a
Gaussian-derived versus purely zonal band-weight parameterization (a four-band
approximation, not a continuous distance function) [@McGrail2012], variable urban and
rural catchments that widen the effective catchment for rural populations
[@McGrail2009], and a modified two-step specification that penalizes suboptimally
configured supply (M2SFCA) [@Delamater2013]. The M2SFCA second application of the
distance weight is intentional and method-specific, not the inadvertent reuse of the
same weights in both steps cautioned against elsewhere [@Zhang2023trap]; a fully
dynamic variable-catchment implementation would expand each catchment until a
population and provider criterion is met rather than compositing separate fixed urban
and rural surfaces [@Luo2012var]. The four listed values are cumulative-band weights
$W_b$ (applied to the population reachable within band $b$); they enter the
computation as incremental band weights $w'_b = W_b - W_{b+1}$ (with $W$ beyond the
outermost band set to 0), which makes the cumulative-isochrone implementation
equivalent to a ring-based E2SFCA. In the first step, each physician location $j$
receives a provider-to-population ratio
$$R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_b w'_b\, P_{jb}},$$
where $S_j$ is the subspecialist supply at $j$ and $P_{jb}$ is the female population
reachable from $j$ within band $b$. In the second step, the accessibility at demand
cell $i$ is the band-weighted sum of the ratios of all physician locations whose
band-$b$ catchment contains $i$,
$$A_i = \sum_{j}\sum_{b} w'_b\, R_j .$$
Supply $S_j$ is the count of distinct active subspecialists (unique National
Provider Identifiers) whose practice location maps to $j$. A quality-control check
confirmed that every physician had exactly one active practice location in each
study year, so supply reflects one physician-equivalent per physician and no
multisite duplication occurred; had a physician held multiple locations the
estimator would have counted them fully at each, so fractional (1/$k$) allocation
would be required only for an extension of the cohort to multisite practice
(Limitations). Accessibility
is a relative index expressed as subspecialists per 100,000 women; it is not a raw
physician-to-population density and is not directly numerically comparable with
distance-based accessibility scores [@Desjardins2023]. We also express it as a
Spatial Access Ratio normalized to the national population-weighted mean of 1.00,
with values above 1 indicating better-than-average spatial access [@Wan2012spar];
the absolute per-100,000 index is retained alongside it so that normalization cannot
conceal changes in the absolute national supply-demand balance.

A structural property of the two-step method is important for interpretation.
Because the same band weights enter both steps, the population-weighted mean of the
accessibility surface over *all* demand reduces algebraically to the total supply
divided by the total population,
$$\frac{\sum_i P_i A_i}{\sum_i P_i}=\frac{\sum_j R_j\sum_i w'_{ij}P_i}{\sum_i P_i}=\frac{\sum_j S_j}{\sum_i P_i},$$
which we verified numerically (the national means in Table 1 equal
subspecialist counts per 100,000 women to within 0.02%). The *national*
mean is therefore a **standardized supply-per-population index** and carries no
spatial information; the across-subspecialty ranking it induces is the
workforce-size ranking. Spatial variation is expressed only in the *distribution* of
the surface, the rurality and race/ethnicity contrasts, the share of the population
outside the modeled catchment, and geographic inequality, which we accordingly treat
as the primary spatial outcomes. National means and their ranking are reported as
standardized workforce measures, not as spatial accessibility.

## eResults S5: Disparities across all subspecialties {-}

Viewed across all seven specialty groups, the disparity pattern was consistent
(Figure 4). In 2020, rural women had lower potential accessibility than
metropolitan women for every subspecialty, by as much as
`r pp1(abs(rural_worst_pct))`% for `r full_name[rural_worst]` and by at least
`r pp1(abs(rural_min_pen))`% even for the least affected subspecialty. American
Indian or Alaska Native women had lower accessibility than non-Hispanic White women for `r n_aian_worse` of the seven specialty groups. By contrast, Black,
Hispanic, Asian, and Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander women generally
had higher modeled accessibility than non-Hispanic White women, reflecting their
greater concentration in metropolitan areas where subspecialists practice, a pattern
of potential proximity that, as discussed below, does not imply equivalent realized
access or outcomes. These spatial patterns were robust to the modeling assumptions:
in a sensitivity analysis that varied the distance-decay weights, the catchment
bands, and the grid resolution, the rural disadvantage held for all `r sens_n`
subspecialties under every specification, and the rural and race contrasts moved in
magnitude but never reversed in direction (Appendix Table S2).

```{r fig_equity_hm}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig_equity_heatmap.jpg"))
```
**Figure 4.** Potential accessibility for disadvantaged groups relative to their
reference group in 2020, across all seven specialty groups. Each cell is the percent
difference in 2020 population-weighted accessibility between a group and its
reference group *within* that subspecialty:
red = at least 10% lower access, blue = at least 10% higher, gray = within ±10%.
Reference groups: rurality, metropolitan; race and ethnicity, non-Hispanic White.
Within-subspecialty relative contrasts facilitate comparison across subspecialties
of differing scarcity, but should be interpreted cautiously where absolute
accessibility is low (for example, complex family planning and pediatric and
adolescent gynecology), because relative differences become unstable at very small
baseline values. Enhanced two-step floating catchment area access per 100,000
women;
tract-level population-weighted; contiguous United States. AIAN, American Indian or
Alaska Native; NHOPI, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander.

## eResults S6: Persistence of disparities over time {-}

Rural and racial disparities persisted across the decade (Figure 5; Appendix
Table S1). Over `r first_year`-`r primary_last`, the metropolitan-to-rural
gynecologic oncology accessibility ratio narrowed by
`r sprintf("%.3f", abs(go_ratio_trend[["slope"]]))` per year
(`r fmt_p_txt(go_ratio_trend[["p_ols"]])`; Newey-West
`r fmt_p_txt(go_ratio_trend[["p_hac"]])`), and the American Indian or Alaska Native
zero-access share for gynecologic oncology declined by
`r sprintf("%.2f", abs(gtr("GO","AIAN")$slope_pp_yr))` percentage points per year
(`r fmt_p_txt(gtr("GO","AIAN")$p_ols)`; Newey-West
`r fmt_p_txt(gtr("GO","AIAN")$p_hac)`) while remaining the highest of any group in
every year. Directions were unchanged under autocorrelation-robust inference,
although with only 10 annual estimates the trend tests are imprecise (Appendix
Table S1).

```{r fig4}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig4_gotrends.jpg"))
```

isochrones). (A) Mean accessibility by rurality. (B) Mean accessibility by race and
ethnicity, with American Indian or Alaska Native (AIAN), non-Hispanic White, and
Asian groups highlighted and the remaining groups in gray. (C) Share of each
group’s population living in census tracts with zero mean modeled access.

## eResults S7: Access deserts across subspecialties {-}

The magnitude of inaccessibility depended strongly on subspecialty scarcity
(Figure 6; Table 3). The rural zero-access share ranged from about `r pp1(rural_zero_min)`% for `r rural_zero_min_sub`
to about `r pp1(rural_zero_max)`% for `r rural_zero_max_sub`, and was consistently highest for American Indian or Alaska
Native women (Table 3). These tract-level, travel-time patterns parallel
the
county-level, distance-based gynecologic oncology access disparities reported by
Desjardins and colleagues [@Desjardins2023].

```{r fig5}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(figdir, "fig5_equity.jpg"))
```
**Figure 6.** Change in the share of (A) rural and (B) American Indian or Alaska
Native women living in census tracts with zero mean modeled access, by
subspecialty, `r first_year`→`r primary_last`. The gray dot marks the `r first_year`
value and the arrowhead the `r primary_last` value, so the arrow's length is the
absolute change and its head shows the direction; blue arrows indicate an
improvement (falling zero-access share) and red arrows a worsening, with the
absolute change (percentage points) labeled. Tract-level population-weighted;
enhanced two-step floating catchment area on 30/60/120/180-minute isochrones;
contiguous United States.
